predictions.text: Question About Disclosure Day. Overall I enjoyed the film. But one of the things that seemed like such an oversight to me was that the aliens only seemed to have landed in the USA? It kind of seems a little lazy to me, especially since Close Encounters does have an international focus to it. Am I mistaken? Did they mention other countries where aliens landed? Is this Spielberg's way of communicating some kind of commentary or was it just because it didn't seem like a big deal for the sake of a blockbuster movie?

Ken Russell's The Devils. I don't know what to say other than it is amazing. I never heard of this movie before. It just popped up on Rotten Tomatoes as a theatrical re-release. It got great reviews so decided to watch it. It has that The Holy Mountain Vibe that I love. Made in 1971. I found it on the Movie Vault App on Roku. I give it a solid 8/10.

I'm not sure which True Grit I like better. I rewatched this for the first time since 2010. I also rewatched the original John Wayne movie before my rewatch. I think both movies are pretty great. I was surprised how many lines in the 2010 movie were ripped directly from the original. I think the casting and performances in the 2010 movie were very good, probably better than the original, overall. I do think that the original has better filming locations and a better color palette. I didn't like the change, in the remake, that has Maddie kill Chaney with the Sharps instead of her father's Colt. Both movies foreshadow the gun being too large for her to handle. When she kills Chaney with the Colt, the recoil makes her stumble into the pit. The new movie does have her stumble into the creek from the Colt recoil when she shoots Chaney the first time, but I felt that having it happen with the killing and the pit was more fitting. I did like that the new movie let LaBeouf live (apparently this is true to the book) instead of anti-climatically dying, like in the first movie.

I decided to watch this movie for the first time, and I found it truly heartbreaking to witness the struggles of a couple trying to repair their marriage. It was emotional to see two people fighting to save their relationship while dealing with the problems that had driven them apart. I believe Dean has the potential to become a better man and a better husband. It's clear that he loves and cares for his daughter, Frankie, but his drinking habits are holding him back from becoming the person he could be. It's heartbreaking to see how his personal struggles and poor choices take a toll on his marriage and family, especially when there is still so much at stake. This is one of the reasons why I have always been against drinking and rarely drink alcohol myself. I believe excessive drinking can contribute to negative behaviour, poor decision-making, and domestic problems that can damage relationships and hurt the people we love. To me, a healthy relationship requires mutual respect, understanding, communication, and a willingness to take responsibility for our actions. Sometimes, saving a marriage means confronting our personal struggles before they destroy the very things that matter most in life.

Obsession. Why are people so obsessed with obsession? Going to the theatre with such hype all around and a global box office success, this was one of the most unsatisfactory watches in a long time. The movie wasn't absolutely bad. It was a decent movie. But something didn't satisfy. Just got out of the theatre and still trying to organize the reasons for that. One I can quickly think or feel is the movie was rushed at some points and dragging at some points. Not consistent at all. Am I the only one who feels this way?

Directors Whose Earlier Work Makes You Look at Them in a Completely Different Light? My first exposure to the films of Jonathan Demme was THE SILENCE OF THE LAMBS and PHILADELPHIA. As such, I had thought of him as the maker of serious dramas. But a few months ago I finally watched Demme's SOMETHING WILD (1986), which I loved. What I didn't expect was how wacky both SOMETHING WILD and MARRIED TO THE MOB (1988) are and just how adept Demme seemed to be at directing comedy. Those two movies completely opened my eyes. Has anyone had a similar experience watching a different filmmaker's earlier output, where you had previously thought of them as strictly making movies of a particular sort, but subsequently realized they were more versatile than you had originally thought?

James Gray's We Own the Night is severely underrated. If you think The Godfather is a masterpiece, then you should absolutely love James Gray's We Own the Night. This film explores devotion to family and morality and personal ethics in much the same way as The Godfather. Joaquin Phoenix's character arc is the inverse of Michael Corleone's arc. He starts in a criminal underworld and his family pulls him into law enforcement, and it ends with the same melancholy that the Godfather reserves for Michael becoming the head of a crime family. James Gray's first three films are all incredibly Coppola-esque but We Own the Night is the best of the bunch. I'm fascinated by its tepid response when it came out so hope it gets a reappraisal.

Classic era examples of competency porn films. I recently watched "One of Our Aircraft Is Missing (1942)" and ended up really enjoying the film, especially its depiction of the dedication, resolve, and planning of the Dutch that end up assisting the bomber crew in their mission to return home. We see the Dutch construct a highly sophisticated underground network to assist their allies, all without the Germans understanding they are constantly being lied to. It certainly fits into the competency porn category from that perspective. After watching this, I wanted to see other examples of the competency porn categorization of older films, but most lists I found ended up only really including newer movies, with almost no representation of anything prior to that. What are some other films that fit this genre that are older? (Mainly interested in classic and silent film eras, so pre 70s).

"The Odyssey" is far from the visual treat I was expecting. While I was watching it, all I could think of was this did not look like the work of a confident director, but of someone that's (way too) confident in his 'directorial brand'. The shots at sea, for instance, are screaming for the audience to be in awe of the technical difficulties. But other than a couple of standout sequences, namely the superbly staged act featuring Samantha Morton as Circe, the movie itself is visually unremarkable and below Nolan's standards. The visual symmetry of "Dunkirk" is gone. The battle scenes are generically choreographed, and the mise en scène was lacking even in crucial interior shots, including the climax. I'll mention one element of the picture that clearly stands out: the elegance and precision of Ludwig Göransson's score, which Nolan's directorial achievement never quite matches.

There are some interesting horror movies hitting theaters tomorrow (10/16) so which one are you going to? Ken Russell's The Devils, You Can't Leave, One Eye Open, Nayyi Navelli. I've heard some buzz about each, so curious where everyone is going. For me, Devils is on the list and You Can't Leave. What about y'all?

How do you like to watch movies? Another discussion got me thinking; how do people like to watch movies? And I don't mean 'at the cinema' vs 'at home'. If going out to watch a movie, do you prefer Old-school theatre, Modern multiplex, 2D, 3D, Screen X, 4DX, Imax, some other version? Or perhaps the drive-in, outdoor cinema, waterpark movies? If you like a mix, how do you decide what should be seen in which format? As for me, I love the cinema. The bigger the action movie, the bigger the screen. I will choose the big screen over at home almost every time. 3D for the movies made with it in mind, but NEVER 4DX. I LOVED the Drive-in. That was my favourite. Sadly, they no longer exist in my country now. My favourite cinema has something like it. Two theatres have VW vehicles in them, so it kind of feels like the drive-in.

Why does no one ever talk about The Cranes Are Flying? The Cranes Are Flying got a hell of a résumé: Palme d'Or Winner; routinely showing up on "Greatest Films Of All Time" lists; ranked Top 32 on letterboxd. I have never encountered a single discussion, article or video about this film unless I actively sought it out. It's very emotionally potent and relatable, it's visually INCREDIBLE, politically fascinating given when and where it was made. So I'm curious: Is it because Soviet cinema outside of Tarkovsky, Eisenstein and Klimov has never really entered the broader cinephile spaces? Is it overshadowed by Come and See so people think "it's just another Soviet anti-war film"? What do you think about the movie? Do you agree with this at all or does this apply to plenty more movies of the same caliber and I'm just biased?

Actors that you thought would become big after watching them in an early role for the first time? I recall watching Miss Stevens in 2017, and Timothee Chalamet's monologue made me go "Wow! What an actor!" Another example is Carey Mulligan in Doctor Who, she starred in my favourite episode of the show (Blink). The episode is a masterpiece but I was particularly impressed by how Mulligan carried that episode. Can you recall any actors who, the first time you saw them in an early role, made you think they are going to kill it in the industry?

Matt Damon as Odysseus was a massive miscast. I just watched the new Odyssey adaptation, and Matt Damon's performance was deeply disappointing. It stripped away everything that makes Odysseus such a complex, deeply human character. Homer depicts Odysseus as the ultimate master tactician, whose calm voice fell "like snowflakes in winter." Damon completely missed this magnetic charm and sharp mind, playing him as bland, passive, and frankly unintelligent. Instead of showing calculating brilliance, this version makes him look reckless and downright foolish through bizarre choices, like shooting the Cyclops with an arrow or recklessly confronting Antinous head on instead of using his trademark patience and disguise. Did anyone else feel this way, or do you place the blame more on the screenplay than on Damon himself?

Lav Diaz's Melancholia (2008). I saw Melancholia and it clocks in at 447 minutes which is close to 8 hours long. As I sit with Melancholia's credits, I was left surprisingly moved. There's a part where the rebel fighters are trekking to the forest, hiding from the military, and as it goes on they lose grip of their sanity. A rebel named Renato Munoz writes to his wife that there is no point to this sadness anymore, he can no longer romanticize this pain, it's all senseless brutality. Because of sadness, there is cinema, there is painting, there is poetry and it has no cure, one character says. The locations take you from mountains, to beaches, to the city, to interiors of old houses, to jungles. There's also three characters we start the film with, a sex worker, a nun, and a pimp, and the film then reveals that it is a psychodrama therapy session formed by the pimp to alleviate and heal their past traumas.

Broadcast News (1987). I despise James L. Brooks (as a director). I have never hated two movies more than Broadcast News and Terms of Endearment. Broadcast News is the biggest blowjob to media cretins and to upper-middle class strivers in general. I've met people over the years for which Broadcast News is their favorite movie. When they say that, it's like peaking behind the curtain. Not only do they find these lizards "flawed yet relatable" or "charming", they really want to live in that world. It's a sitcom world where everyone is manic and trades lame quips and zingers.

The end of inception is an insanely accurate representation of waking from a rough dream. Like, holy crap i felt the intensity every minute through. I still knew it was a big heist in a dream but as someone who has vivid dreams, cobb waking up on the plane in distress only to be met with the flight attendant "do you need immigration forms sir?" "Thank you" Its insanely accurate. The whole plot is based around this intense dream and after going through hell and back, lo and behold, you're awake. Back to normal. I know in-universe cobb got home to his kids and destroyed Fischer's empire, so it had HUGE repercussions. It wasnt really just a dream. But the whole concept of a dream was fleshed out unbelievably well in this movie. You know its bs, it fleshes the plot out so you forget its bs and take it seriously-- THEN BAM. You're woken up on a flight.

Why does Lawrence of Arabia (1962) feel much more modern than Bridge on the River Kwai (1957)? I saw Bridge on the River Kwai for the first time last night, and loved it. But one thing that struck me is that despite being made only 5 years prior to Lawrence of Arabia, it feels a lot more old-fashioned. They're both excellent films, made by the same director, and they're both war films. But despite the similarities, with Lawrence I feel like I'm watching an early film from the modern era, but I didn't get that with Kwai at all. Was it the acting style, the cinematography, or something else? What makes a film feel modern to you?

Movies or Shows that depict living life with PTSD. I really liked The Falcon and the Winter Soldier's depiction of Bucky's PTSD. It showed him genuinely trying to connect with people, get mental help, and work on himself, and how hard this is with PTSD. I want more shows or movies that aren't a super depressing self pity fest depicting life after trauma. I want to see the protagonist live life with their PTSD, not despite of it. Where the character works on themself and with the other people around them, and in the end has a happy ending where they have friends, community, and still get the help they need.

The Beyond (1981) feels less like Hell invading reality and more like reality slowly becoming Hell. What interests me most about The Beyond is how space gradually stops making sense. At first, the supernatural is tied to specific places: the hotel, the gateway, certain rooms. But by the end, John and Liza leave the hospital and somehow end up back at the hotel, then enter the wasteland where every direction leads nowhere. That makes me wonder if the film's apparent incoherence is partly deliberate. Maybe Hell isn't simply another place they enter. Maybe reality itself is losing causality, distance, and direction. Do you think that makes the film's loose narrative more effective, or is that reading too generous to Fulci?

My Problem with Nolan, The Odyssey and Why Dark Knight was the WORST Thing to Happen to Him. Nolan's strength is plot, and having story-driven movies that are more self contained. This is why he still has not made films as good as Memento and Prestige because those films play to his strengths. So now we have The Dark Knight, where despite how it helped to elevate the Superhero movie and gave us one of the great characters in Joker, the main character was weak and not well written, the fight choreography was incredibly weak and the exposition led to a very derivative story that TOLD more than it SHOWED. The immense success of that film made Nolan think he should be making big event, blockbuster films that rely on dynamic visuals and more elaborate action scenes - two aspects that Nolan is not strong at. So when we come to the Odyssey, you see how the visuals are drab, the action scenes are lacking and you don't really connect with Odysseus in the way David Lean made us go on a journey with Lawrence or Maximus in Gladiator.

A more disturbing version of Obsession? What if Bear got his real wish? I think the general consensus is that this is a film about violation of consent which showcases Bear's actions as morally wrong. But one thing that stood out to me was that the willow failed to deliver Bear's actual wish. Bear wished for Nikki to love him, but in fact she never did. I would like to propose a retelling where instead of subjugating her conscious mind, the willow wish instead rewires Nikki's brain and causes her to truly love Bear, through and through. In this version, Bear still commits the evil act of using magic power to force a woman's consent, but there is no bizarre behavior nor overt horror that follows, and no negative consequences for Bear. This version would be difficult to market as a horror film, and yet this story is perhaps more sinister and deeply disturbing than the original. The villain wins and his victim is happy that he did.

On Obsession obsession. I saw Obsession opening weekend and like many was very impressed. I think it's a fantastic performance from Navarette and will undoubtedly make her a star, but I still had some issues with the male lead and some of the storytelling. Overall it was a very promising indie debut. All that said, I've been a little baffled by the response to it. A film of this scale outgrossing something like Sinners is admittedly a little surprising. I teach at a film school and have been asking my students about it, and none of my undergrad or graduate aged students seem to have more than a mild appreciation for it. I stumbled across the subreddit for the film this week and found people obsessively discussing fan theories and declaring it the greatest film in years. Does anyone else have any insights as to what exactly this movie has tapped into to get what I'm assuming are teens to the theater week over week for two months now? It's become an academic curiosity for me.

The Aviator made me realize why Nolan doesn't hold a candle to Scorsese. Finally got around to filling in one of my last blanks in Scorsese's filmography. It seems like the sort of movie Nolan thinks he made with Oppenheimer and, in some ways, The Odyssey. What sets Scorsese apart, however, is that, while there is certainly identification with the subject, there is far less reverence. Nolan's troubled geniuses often feel flat to me because whatever their faults, I'm ultimately always expected to admire them. Less so with Marty's deeply fucked up, perverted misfits. Travis Bickle, Jake La Motta, Jordan Belfort and Howard Hughes all have traits in common, and yet they are far more diverse than the likes of John Cobb, Bruce Wayne, Oppenheimer and Odysseus. Nolan uses his art to come to grips with his own obsessions and neuroses, Scorsese tries to understand the world around him.

Title really says it's all but essentially look for films that women usually hate and men love, maybe like a wolf of wall street style vibe. The more male coded the film would be better, imagine movies that a group of guys would watch together and everyone would be engaged. I guess for the opposite you could have the notebook.

I'm a fan of dogs, specifically dogs... and dog movies. But today's question I have is, whatever happened to the "A Dogs Purpose" franchise? The author's book was adapted to the screen in 2017, with a film that from my own neighborhood I could tell was popular, EVERYONE'S DOG was named Bailey. Then in 2018 Sony did "A Dog's Way Home" another book from him, with a movie I love, and finally in 2019 the sequel to Purpose, "A Dog's Journey" which I also love and think is a darker film then the first with some of the subject matter. But since then nothing until apparently 5 days ago when Netflix posted a trailer for "A Dog's Perfect Christmas" also by the same author. and I just saw this and it made me want to ask... "where's the third A Dog's Purpose?" I'm gonna guess it's one of the following: A. Box office failure of the sequel- tho I ask how much did the sequel costs / lose? B. Animal Abuse Allegations of the first leading to bad PR? But then... why did the first do so well? I'm just confused and sad, because I'd love to see the story's "continuation"... whatever it is, I want the final chapter. But it's not been made yet. Anyone got insights?

Thoughts on Brazil? I re-watched Brazil and I really loved the film. It is most definitely a Terry Gilliam film. Every scene in the film is just perfection and every scene is just so surreal and original. The acting is great as well. Jonathan Pryce was great as Sam Lowry and DeNiro honestly surprised me with his role as Harry Tuttle. Kim Greist was okay as Jill, but I was indifferent with her performance. I also know about the behind the scenes conflicts with the film, with Gilliam struggling to get the film released in the USA and Universal making a "Love Conquers All" Cut before shelving the film entirely. I haven't seen the Love Conquers All Cut and I wonder how different it is. I also think a good companion piece for Brazil is 1984 with John Hurt. What are your thoughts on Brazil? What do you think of the Love Conquers All Cut and how different is it from Gilliam's Cut?

All Dogs Go To Heaven... any chance the Bluth cut (PG) cut gets released? All Dogs Go To Heaven is my favorite Bluth film, its dark, yet heartwarming, it's afterlife scenarios are intense yet tied together with a theme of redemption. The available edit is trimmed to remove the hell scene's most frightening bits, one use of the word damn and supposedly Charlie actually getting run over... which I do wonder if that actually exist due to the choppy edit in the final cut. Is there ANY chance this exists? Is it long gone? A lost myth? Bluth's said it's gone, but isn't there an HD still? Could it be remade with A.I and "re-edited back in"? AND SECOND QUESTION: Who even owns the rights to the film?

Like the main final line, indescribable chatter afterwards I don't count. Silence of the lambs "I'm having an old friend for dinner" is a strong contender. Naturally Casablanca with the friendship line is iconic, but there must be some modern classics I can't think of. Beauty killed the best is another classic but quite an old one too

Trivia of the Week: Constance Miller was already in the shop when McCabe went to buy three girls for $200 in McCabe & Mrs. Miller (1971). Do you ever wonder how Constance Miller suddenly shows up and starts talking McCabe into letting her manage the whorehouse? Well, it's kind of a cool, blink-and-you'll-miss-it detail, but she's already inside the shop in Bearpaw (the next town) when McCabe goes to buy three girls for $200 from the pimp. You can spot Mrs. Miller just inside the doorway when the pimp briefly opens it to bring one of the whores out. McCabe doesn't meet her then, but she must've either learned about him from the pimp or overheard the pimp say, "You don't know what you're doing, McCabe. You got no experience at this." Even in that brief glimpse, you see her rubbing her nose. What does that tell you? She must be on something.

Who saw The Exorcist (1973) in theaters? Curious to hear any personal accounts of what it was like to experience The Exorcist for the first time, including the lead-up to the actual release. I've always been fascinated by the lore that the original theatrical trailer made people physically ill (there is a ton of flashing), to the point Warner Bros. eventually pulled it. This film is still terrifying to me today, so I can't imagine how I would have reacted back then!

anyone fond of Hal Hartley's works? I just saw his film "Meanwhile" which was my 9th film of his filmography and I gotta say he's spot on 9 for 9 thus far. It's actually incredible stuff, I've never encountered a more consistent filmography. Every single film has a stark script that's both sardonic, sincere at the same time. I'm curious why he didn't end up receiving the same fame as his other contemporary indie filmmakers like Jarmusch or Tarantino. His style is one of a kind.

[Contains Spoilers] Trains Dreams was a beautiful movie. Brilliant Acting. But I simply do not believe the narrator at the end. "But on that Spring day, as he misplaced all sense of up and down, he felt at last, connected to it all." Robert Grainier spent close to forty years of his life lonely, rudderless, and miserable. Am I really supposed to believe that it was all worth it because in the end he gets to take a 10 minute plane ride before he dies? I call bullshit. This was a man who desperately craved a scrap of goodness in his life. I think he imagined a sense of connection because he wanted it so badly that he was able to fool even himself for a moment. Here is a man who knew his life was complete shit and did almost nothing about it for 40ish years. Instead he sat in his cabin, alone in the woods, staring at the wall every damn night. All he did was wait for something to happen, until it never did. Don't be like Robert. How else could you possibly interpret the second half of his life?

Andy Warhol's Flesh (1968). I was surprised to find this movie had largely negative reviews both contemporarily and retrospectively. I loved it. It's mildly hammy, amateurish, lacking in plot. It's inhabited by various famous figures from the 'Warhol set' of 1960s New York, including Joe Dallesandro, Candy Darling, Jackie Curtis. The plot centers on Joe and his wife Geri needing to make $200 so they can pay for Geri's girlfriend's abortion, both of them sex workers. The director's explanation of the movie was that it's about all of the problems people have in relation to their flesh - the problem of having to sell your flesh to live, of having to bear flesh, of aging flesh, of being born with the 'wrong flesh'. The lines are blurred by the fact that many of the characters are essentially playing hammed up versions of themselves - Joe Dallesandro was a real-life sex worker and male model, for example, and drew from real-life experiences for his performance.
